slides.note: Define the release contract and identify the evidence required to approve a change. slides.title: LLMOps controls behavior across releases
body: Quality and safety need baselines, owners and release gates.
Latency, failures and tokens need measured operating limits.
Every change needs evidence, an approver and a rollback path.
slides.note: Use the Friday-to-Monday failure story to identify which artifact changed and who owns it. Evaluate a model candidate on the same task and evaluation scope as the baseline, considering task quality, safety, latency, cost and compatibility. A hosted model can change behavior without an application code change, so retain model/provider metadata and comparison evidence. Today establishes the control contract; endpoint tuning, gateway policies and detailed FinOps are developed in later sessions. Primary syllabus: LLMOps_Syllabus.md sections 01, 03, 08, 14. body: Record model/provider ID, owner, purpose and approval state.
Benchmark candidates on one frozen dataset and configuration.
Check compatibility; retain a rollback bundle before retirement.

Compare baseline and candidate under the same dataset, task, prompt and retrieval scope, and check structured output, tool schema, token limits and embedding compatibility as applicable. A migration plan retains the previous prompt, configuration, corpus and compatible embedding/index/parent stores until rollback is validated; automated promotion and retirement are design work here. slides.title: Four phases / explicit release decisions
slides.note: Use Discover, Distill, Deploy and Deliver as checkpoints for the syllabus lifecycle rather than as an application-building tutorial. Discover records permitted data and owners; Distill compares a candidate with a frozen baseline; Deploy checks compatibility and measured service limits; Deliver watches production and exercises rollback. A valid thresholds file is only configuration validation, and offline fixtures do not approve production quality or capacity. slides.title: Governance / three independent checks
body: Freshness: does indexed evidence match the approved source?
Permission: may this scope access and disclose the content?
Audit: can a reviewer recover versions and the decision?
slides.note: Treat freshness, authorization and auditability as independent controls. The source register and checksums establish byte identity, while effective dates, access policies and provider data rules answer different questions. Record the data owner, provider disclosure decision, retention and residency requirements, access-review owner and the evidence required for retirement. Configured metadata filters and redaction help enforce boundaries but are not proof of authenticated per-user authorization or complete sensitive-data detection. body: Cases: normal, refusal, date boundary, adversarial
Compare: same dataset, rubric and release identities
Reference checks + a calibrated judge + human review.
Record disagreements; keep candidate tuning apart from the holdout.

Calibrate an LLM judge against human labels, inspect disagreement and bias, and version the rubric; no judge calls or measured model-quality claims are part of this offline lab. body: In a temporary copy: set faithfulness_min=1.5; expect INVALID.
Valid + status=placeholder means HOLD for production approval.

slides.title: Code / reject changed source bytes
body: def _verify_source(path: Path, entry: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
"""Refuse a file whose bytes differ from the register's recorded sha256."""
raise ValueError(f"{entry['doc_id']}: file sha256 does not match the document register")
A source must match the register before parsing or embedding.
slides.note: Read the exact _verify_source excerpt and identify the validation boundary before parsing or embedding. The SHA-256 comparison rejects changed bytes against the registered source identity and supports an audit trail. A matching hash does not establish permission, freshness, policy correctness or approval to send text to an external provider. Keep those decisions as separate evidence in the inventory and governance worksheet. Primary syllabus: LLMOps_Syllabus.md sections 09, 10, 12. body: Candidate lacks quality and compatibility evidence → HOLD.
Name approver, rollback bundle, trigger and retirement condition.

The expected decision is HOLD; list the missing checks, decide who can approve, and retain the old prompt, model/configuration and compatible corpus, embeddings, index and parent collections. body: Hand in: inventory, baseline cases and two failure transcripts.
Defend: owner, evidence, HOLD or promote, rollback target.
Pass the exercise; keep unmeasured production gates open.

Ask each pair to defend its HOLD decision for the provider-change case and identify the owner and missing evidence that could change it. slides.title: Measure latency, usage and failure signals
body: Syllabus 04, 05, 08, 14 / Fixtures and live exercises labeled / sources and lab steps in notes
Stage duration + request p50/p95/p99; TTFT/TPOT need token timestamps.
Input/output/cached tokens, actual model/backend and measured unit cost.
Timeout / rate limit / retrieval miss / schema error / invalid citation.
slides.note: Measure request and stage durations, and compute percentiles over repeated observations rather than a single trace. Track input, output and cached-token fields when the provider reports them, plus the selected model and retry/fallback attempts; local inference still consumes hardware resources. The current answer endpoint is buffered JSON, so TTFT and TPOT remain unmeasured without streaming instrumentation. Model errors, missing evidence and unsafe/invalid output have different operational owners, and query redaction alone does not prove all automatically captured trace fields are sanitized. Primary syllabus: LLMOps_Syllabus.md sections 04, 05, 08, 14; full practicals: training/session2/handout.md and training/session2/live_practicals.md.

slides.title: EvalOps / build the evaluation harness
body: Syllabus 02, 03, 05, 11 / Fixtures and live exercises labeled / sources and lab steps in notes
slides.note: The harness freezes cases, runs a versioned candidate, captures contexts and answers, scores them, applies gates and records a human decision. Reuse app/evaluation/run.py and its RagasScorer adapter rather than inventing a second production evaluator. Include normal, refusal, date-boundary, adversarial and missing-evidence cases; preserve the holdout and case identities across comparisons. Judges are stochastic and require human-label calibration, bias review and an explicit rubric before automatic scores justify release decisions. slides.title: Evals / separate coverage from supported claims
body: Syllabus 03, 05, 12 / Fixtures and live exercises labeled / sources and lab steps in notes
Are the answer claims supported by the supplied retrieved context?
Does retrieved evidence cover the claims required by the reference?
Is the answer right for the task, and does it answer the question?
slides.note: Ragas faithfulness assesses support for response claims, while context recall uses reference information to assess missing evidence; neither is the same as the repository reference-ID recall at k. Correctness, relevance and safety require separate criteria, and high faithfulness does not prove that the supplied source is true. Treat one minus faithfulness only as an unsupported-claim proxy, not a calibrated probability that an entire response hallucinated. Sources: https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/faithfulness/ and https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_recall/; DeepEval is an alternative framework rather than another installed scoring pipeline. Primary syllabus: LLMOps_Syllabus.md sections 03, 05, 12; full practicals: training/session2/handout.md and training/session2/live_practicals.md.

Live Ragas: compare Qwen chat with the OpenAI chat alias

slides.title: Practical / fail over, balance and cache
body: Syllabus 07, 08, 09, 14 / Fixtures and live exercises labeled / sources and lab steps in notes
In a temp config, break one chat URL; record attempts and actual fallback.
Use two healthy deployments under one alias; count uncached requests.
Repeat identical synthetic input; confirm a hit from upstream-call evidence.
slides.note: Allow 20 minutes to audit the route/failure matrix offline or run it on instructor-prepared services using training/session2/live_practicals.md. Inject failure only in a temporary gateway config by pointing a backend at an unreachable localhost port; test local-to-OpenAI, the reverse map in a separate config, and exhaustion without circular fallbacks. Demonstrate balancing only with two independent healthy endpoints, and verify cache hits with gateway/upstream evidence rather than latency alone. The lab cache is in memory for one worker, cache isolation must include relevant scope/version semantics before sensitive use, and the deprecated proxy mock_testing_fallbacks flag is not used; sources are the LiteLLM fallback, load-balancing and caching documentation linked in the live guide. body: Syllabus 07, 09, 10, 12 / Fixtures and live exercises labeled / sources and lab steps in notes
slides.note: Keep PII redaction before embedding, model disclosure and trace export, with access checks before evidence use and strict output validation afterwards. Prompt boundaries help preserve instruction/data separation, but malicious instructions inside legitimate prose still need adversarial behavioral tests and constrained tools. Guardrails AI can wrap the existing Pydantic contract, while a NeMo Guardrails policy is an alternative integration with its own evaluation and operational cost. No framework name establishes complete injection defense or authentication; the slide describes control responsibilities and the handout identifies implemented versus additional integrations. Primary syllabus: LLMOps_Syllabus.md sections 07, 09, 10, 12; full practicals: training/session2/handout.md and training/session2/live_practicals.md.

slides.title: Practical / PII and prompt injection defenses
body: Syllabus 03, 09, 10, 12 / Fixtures and live exercises labeled / sources and lab steps in notes
Recognized PII → typed placeholders before disclosure
slides.note: Use part of the 15-minute security block for the existing redaction and prompt-boundary exercises. Recognized email, phone, PAN and Aadhaar patterns are masked, while policy amounts remain unchanged; learners should identify both missed identifiers and false positives. The actual rendered production prompt escapes injected XML and retains the system role, proving a syntax boundary rather than semantic injection immunity. Add direct and retrieved-document injection cases to the behavioral evaluation matrix and retain least-privilege, authorization and data-disclosure decisions as separate controls. slides.title: A prompt has three responsibilities

Evidence boundary: which supplied text supports claims.

body: Wrap untrusted content with explicit boundaries.

Keep privileged instructions outside the data field.

slides.title: The sandwich pattern repeats a narrow rule
body: Give scope and grounding instructions before the data.
Place the question inside its declared data boundary.
End with a reminder to follow the output contract.

A tiny negation can reverse an otherwise similar answer.
Use semantic criteria plus deterministic contract checks.

slides.title: Security, Compliance, and Responsible Operation in LLMOps
slides.note: This section follows the lesson Security, Compliance, and Responsible Operation in LLMOps. Teach the concept first, then distinguish the existing NexaAssist implementation from proposed extensions. The slides paraphrase the source rather than reproduce its text. slides.title: Grounded output can still be unsafe
body: A source may contain private information.
A user may request an unauthorized disclosure.
A safe-looking request can consume excessive resources.
slides.note: Correctness and safety are different dimensions. A faithful reproduction of restricted information is still a privacy problem. The source organizes its security discussion around input, output and resource controls. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/security-compliance-and-responsible-operation-in-llmops.
slides.lesson_title: Security, Compliance, and Responsible Operation in LLMOps

slides.title: Recognize direct and indirect injection
body: Direct: the user tries to override the assistant’s rules.
Indirect: retrieved material contains hostile instructions.
Defend at data, prompt, authorization and output boundaries.
slides.note: Do not teach a list of forbidden words as complete injection protection. Text can be phrased or encoded many ways. Retrieved documents are untrusted data even when their surrounding system is useful. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/security-compliance-and-responsible-operation-in-llmops.
slides.lesson_title: Security, Compliance, and Responsible Operation in LLMOps

slides.title: Risk names are stable; numbering is versioned
body: The lesson uses older OWASP LLM01 / LLM04 / LLM06 labels.
OWASP 2025 maps disclosure to LLM02 and consumption to LLM10.
Record the list version when naming a risk.
slides.note: Verified against https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/ on 2026-10-23. Prompt injection remains LLM01:2025. Explain the source’s historical numbering without presenting it as the current taxonomy. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/security-compliance-and-responsible-operation-in-llmops.
slides.lesson_title: Security, Compliance, and Responsible Operation in LLMOps

slides.title: Layer the controls around generation
body: Before: validate, quota and redact the query.
During: bound context and output tokens.
After: detect PII and verify cited quotes.
slides.note: These controls reduce distinct risks. None demonstrates complete injection resistance, data-loss prevention or semantic correctness. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/security-compliance-and-responsible-operation-in-llmops.
slides.lesson_title: Security, Compliance, and Responsible Operation in LLMOps

slides.title: Reuse the query PII rail
body: scrub_request runs before embeddings and generation.
The same pattern engine masks corpus identifiers.
Regex misses names and addresses and can misclassify digits.
slides.note: These are known limits, not a promise of complete compliance. Real data needs an approved privacy policy and evidence appropriate to its risk. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/security-compliance-and-responsible-operation-in-llmops.

slides.title: New / block detected PII before returning

Check answer text and evidence quotes; return the existing safe abstention. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/security-compliance-and-responsible-operation-in-llmops.

slides.title: Preserve citation integrity when blocking
body: Never rewrite a quote and still call it exact.
On a detected identifier, discard the draft and citations.
Log only the event; never log the sensitive text.
slides.note: The new rail is always applied to generated answer and quote text. Source identities and arbitrary free-form private data are not comprehensively inspected by this pattern detector. Run test_readiness_timeout.py and the answer replay.

body: Patterns cover selected identifiers, not all personal data.
Quotas are per process; proxy behavior affects client identity.
Authorization and retention still need deployment decisions.

Teach the concept first, then distinguish the existing NexaAssist implementation from proposed extensions. The slides paraphrase the source rather than reproduce its text. slides.title: Split response time into useful measurements
body: TTFT: request start until the first output token.
TPS: generation rate after output begins.
End-to-end latency also includes queues and retrieval.
slides.note: A buffered API cannot expose user-visible TTFT from generation_ms. Streaming can improve perceived progress, but does not remove prompt processing or queueing delays. Targets should follow the product’s usage rather than universal numbers. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/inference-infrastructure-hardware-economics-and-latency.
slides.lesson_title: Inference Infrastructure: Hardware, Economics, and Latency

slides.title: Weight memory is only the starting estimate
body: Approximate decimal GB = parameter billions × bytes/parameter.
Scenario: 8B × 2 bytes = 16 GB for FP16 weights.
Reserve additional memory for cache, runtime and concurrency.
slides.note: This is a weight-size lower-bound estimate, not a complete GPU purchase recommendation. Runtimes can shard or offload models; memory layout, kernels and architecture influence feasibility. No hardware performance measurement is supplied. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/inference-infrastructure-hardware-economics-and-latency.
slides.lesson_title: Inference Infrastructure: Hardware, Economics, and Latency

slides.title: Quantization changes the weight budget
body: FP16 uses roughly 2 bytes per parameter.
INT8 uses roughly 1; packed INT4 roughly 0.5.
Quality, kernel support and metadata overhead still matter.
slides.note: Scenario: idealized 8B INT4 weights use about 4 decimal GB before overhead. Quantization is not a guarantee of identical behavior or usable throughput. Re-evaluate the actual model and task after changing precision. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/inference-infrastructure-hardware-economics-and-latency.
slides.lesson_title: Inference Infrastructure: Hardware, Economics, and Latency

slides.title: The KV cache grows with workload shape
body: Longer context requires more cached attention state.
Concurrent sequences increase the live memory footprint.
A model loading successfully does not prove capacity.
slides.note: KV memory depends on layer count, attention layout, sequence length, precision and batch size. Avoid treating a fixed “GB per 4000 tokens” number as universal. Capacity must be measured with the intended context and concurrency. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/inference-infrastructure-hardware-economics-and-latency.
slides.lesson_title: Inference Infrastructure: Hardware, Economics, and Latency

slides.title: API versus self-hosting is a utilization decision
body: API: variable token cost plus provider limits and governance.
Self-hosting: fixed capacity cost plus operating effort.
Compare representative traffic, privacy and reliability needs.
slides.note: Provider quotas, availability and network behavior limit effective scalability; API scale is not unlimited. A steady high-volume workload may justify owned capacity, while a bursty one may not. Use total cost, not token price alone. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/inference-infrastructure-hardware-economics-and-latency.
slides.lesson_title: Inference Infrastructure: Hardware, Economics, and Latency

slides.title: Separate input and output prices in the estimate
body: These are scenario prices, not a current provider quote.
slides.note: Compute input and output cost independently: 500,000 input tokens cost $0.05 and 200,000 output tokens cost $0.10. Multiply by 30 for this illustrative month. Include failed calls, retries, judges and embeddings in a complete estimate. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/inference-infrastructure-hardware-economics-and-latency.
slides.lesson_title: Inference Infrastructure: Hardware, Economics, and Latency

slides.title: Parallelism and batching solve different constraints
body: Replicas distribute requests when a model fits per worker.
Sharding distributes a model that needs multiple devices.
Batching trades queue delay for better resource utilization.
slides.note: The source covers data parallelism, model parallelism and asynchronous batching. None guarantees linear throughput in practice. Observe provider rate limits, memory pressure and per-request latency when tuning concurrency. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/inference-infrastructure-hardware-economics-and-latency.
slides.lesson_title: Inference Infrastructure: Hardware, Economics, and Latency

slides.title: Practical / calculate capacity and spend
body: Verify weight-only estimates and scenario token costs.
Write down the missing cache, runtime and concurrency inputs.
slides.note: The calculation is deterministic and offline. It demonstrates arithmetic and assumptions, not a live hardware sizing or pricing recommendation. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/inference-infrastructure-hardware-economics-and-latency.
slides.lesson_title: Inference Infrastructure: Hardware, Economics, and Latency

slides.title: Measure latency, errors and priced tokens
body: Process metrics do not establish a fleet-wide SLO.
slides.note: Latency uses a rolling window, while request/token counters are cumulative. The teaching checker makes required inputs visible but is not a full production observability backend. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/inference-infrastructure-hardware-economics-and-latency.
slides.lesson_title: Inference Infrastructure: Hardware, Economics, and Latency

slides.title: Streaming needs a separate contract
body: Current answers are buffered and validated as a whole.
Total generation time does not measure TTFT or TPS.
Streaming requires deciding when validated content may leave.
slides.note: TTFT means time to first token; TPS means tokens per second. They are discussed as future metrics rather than inferred from the current generation_ms field. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/inference-infrastructure-hardware-economics-and-latency.
slides.lesson_title: Inference Infrastructure: Hardware, Economics, and Latency

slides.title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production
slides.note: This section follows the lesson Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production. Teach the concept first, then distinguish the existing NexaAssist implementation from proposed extensions. The slides paraphrase the source rather than reproduce its text. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/hosting-serving-and-scaling-llms-in-production.
slides.lesson_title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production

slides.title: Async endpoints still need non-blocking internals
body: Await asynchronous provider and HTTP clients.
FastAPI does not offload every utility called inside async def.
slides.note: The source text overstates automatic threadpool handling. Official FastAPI documentation distinguishes synchronous path operations/dependencies from ordinary utility calls. NexaAssist explicitly uses asyncio.to_thread for synchronous PyMongo work. Reference: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/async/. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/hosting-serving-and-scaling-llms-in-production.
slides.lesson_title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production

slides.title: The API owns a strict contract
body: Pydantic rejects invalid or extra request fields.
Depends injects settings and request controls.
Routers delegate; provider failures become safe 503s.
slides.note: Thin routers keep domain behavior reusable by both API and evaluation paths. Never expose provider exception strings in public responses. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/hosting-serving-and-scaling-llms-in-production.
slides.lesson_title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production

slides.title: Practical 1 / exercise the real API
body: Observe health 200, readiness 503 and invalid input 422.
slides.note: ASGI transport keeps this offline. Settings and dependency behavior are injected, while routing, validation and rate-limit code remain real. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/hosting-serving-and-scaling-llms-in-production.
slides.lesson_title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production

slides.title: A failure should reveal enough to act
slides.note: Ask learners what the UI should show for each status. The existing interface already handles rate-limit feedback separately from unavailable service errors. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/hosting-serving-and-scaling-llms-in-production.
slides.lesson_title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production

slides.title: Dependency injection defines resource ownership
body: Create or cache shared clients with clear lifecycle.
Inject application settings and replace services in tests.
Keep domain logic callable outside HTTP routes.
slides.note: Depends is a wiring mechanism, not a blanket singleton or startup guarantee. Resource ownership must be explicit in lifespan, caches or dependencies. The current service/chain split lets evaluation replay the same logic. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/hosting-serving-and-scaling-llms-in-production.
slides.lesson_title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production

slides.title: Health and readiness answer different questions
body: Neither endpoint proves retrieval or answer quality.
slides.note: The readiness endpoint is intentionally narrower than a live RAG test. A healthy database can still have a missing or stale vector index. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/hosting-serving-and-scaling-llms-in-production.
slides.lesson_title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production

slides.title: New / put a deadline on the driver ping
body: The two-second driver deadline applies to readiness, not ordinary retrieval.
slides.code:
def ping_database(settings: Settings) -> None:
    """Bound the readiness probe without shortening normal query deadlines."""
    with timeout(2):
        _database(settings).command("ping")
slides.note: Open app/database/mongo.py and locate def ping_database. Read the displayed excerpt in context; it is taken directly from the application. The two-second driver deadline applies to readiness, not ordinary retrieval. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/hosting-serving-and-scaling-llms-in-production.
slides.lesson_title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production

slides.title: Package the existing application
body: Inspect locked dependencies, non-root user and probe.
Keep API secrets outside the image build context.
slides.note: This delivery does not claim a fresh container build. The handoff describes an earlier dummy-settings smoke test; learners should rerun their deployment checks in their environment. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/hosting-serving-and-scaling-llms-in-production.
slides.lesson_title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production

slides.title: Practical 3 / inspect operational tests
body: Map a request through FastAPI and workflow spans.
Explain why transport-only API tests omit lifespan.
slides.note: The standalone serving lab does not execute startup. Separate tests cover telemetry initialization, and a live Datadog demo remains optional. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/hosting-serving-and-scaling-llms-in-production.
slides.lesson_title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production

slides.title: A reproducible image still needs safe deployment
body: Freeze dependencies and build with an excluded-secret context.
Inject secrets at runtime; do not COPY .env into images.
Review networking, readiness and rollout in the target platform.
slides.note: The source Docker example includes COPY .env while later advising runtime secrets. The revised training follows the runtime-secret practice and existing dockerignore. No cloud provider deployment is assumed or performed. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/hosting-serving-and-scaling-llms-in-production.
slides.lesson_title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production

slides.title: Cost follows measured tokens
body: Cost = (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price) / 1M.
Monthly estimate = priced query cost × expected query volume.
Verify current provider prices before the live exercise.
slides.note: Use approved prices and a representative request mix. No current model availability or price is asserted by these slides; historical saved prices may be stale. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/hosting-serving-and-scaling-llms-in-production.
slides.lesson_title: Hosting, Serving, and Scaling LLMs in Production

slides.title: Exit gate / can we serve it responsibly?
body: Submit API failure matrix and limitation note.
Define representative staging traffic and approved budgets.
Hold a live release when required SLOs are unmeasured.
slides.note: A fake returning 503 proves error handling. It does not prove readiness recovery, production capacity or model quality under load.

slides.title: Next / detect, investigate and recover
body: Carry the quality and operational evidence forward.
Bring one regression and one misleading feedback item.
slides.note: The operating loop connects traces, reviewed feedback, golden cases and reversible configuration. It begins after deployment rather than ending there.

slides.title: Deliver
slides.note: The final session uses synthetic incidents and actual checkers. Learners must distinguish an exercise decision from a production deployment action. This revised deck follows the course lesson sequence; exact lesson URLs appear in section notes and the coverage map.

slides.title: What the final release file must explain
body: What changed and which artifacts produced the answer.
Which measured gates passed, failed or remain unknown.
Who can approve release and who can restore service.
slides.note: A release file is evidence for a decision, not a decorative checklist. Any missing identifier or unmeasured target stays visible.

slides.title: The last three-hour workshop
body: 25 min operating loop + 20 min trace walkthrough
90 min labs, including a 10 min break
25 min incident review + 20 min final debrief
slides.note: The practicals cover incident metrics, reviewed feedback and a rollback tabletop. Keep time for each pair to defend its release hold or approval recommendation.

slides.title: Showcase / a complaint becomes a test
body: A staff member flags an unhelpful answer.
A reviewer checks sources and accepts the signal.
A separate curated answer becomes a golden case.
slides.note: Acceptance does not authenticate the client response or certify the correction. Export requires the same input, explicit expected status/output and source references for an answered target. Detected PII is blocked.

slides.title: Run the reviewed-feedback demonstration
body: Validate JSONL, keep the review, rehearse recovery.

slides.title: Orchestration and Application Logic
slides.note: This section follows the lesson Orchestration and Application Logic. Teach the concept first, then distinguish the existing NexaAssist implementation from proposed extensions. The slides paraphrase the source rather than reproduce its text. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/orchestration-and-application-logic.
slides.lesson_title: Orchestration and Application Logic

slides.title: Follow-up questions change retrieval requirements
body: A query such as “Does that fee apply earlier?” lacks scope alone.
Conversation history can resolve the subject and date.
Memory adds privacy, latency and correctness obligations.
slides.note: NexaAssist currently asks a standalone policy question per request. Teach the source’s orchestration design without claiming that persistence, rewriting or session authentication exists in production. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/orchestration-and-application-logic.
slides.lesson_title: Orchestration and Application Logic

slides.title: Keep API workers stateless; store conversation state
slides.note: This is the course reference design, not an implemented NexaAssist workflow. A real implementation must authorize session access and isolate users. A worker-local list loses context across replicas and restarts. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/orchestration-and-application-logic.
slides.lesson_title: Orchestration and Application Logic

slides.title: A sliding window is a budget approximation
body: Load a bounded recent history instead of all turns.
Message count is simple but ignores varying token length.
Reserve tokens for instructions, evidence and output.
slides.note: The source illustrates six recent messages. That is a heuristic, not a recommended universal setting. Production history requires deterministic ordering, retention, deletion and a token-aware budget appropriate to the selected model. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/orchestration-and-application-logic.
slides.lesson_title: Orchestration and Application Logic

slides.title: Rewriting must preserve the user’s meaning
body: Resolve references using only authorized recent history.
Keep original question and rewritten search query separate.
Validate output; time out or fall back when rewriting fails.
slides.note: A cheap rewriter is another model call and failure surface. It can change a fee date or invent a product. A fallback to the original question preserves availability but may retrieve poorly; asking for clarification can be safer depending on the contract. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/orchestration-and-application-logic.
slides.lesson_title: Orchestration and Application Logic

slides.title: New state needs multi-turn evaluation
body: Capture history, current input and expected source.
Test incorrect rewrites, missing history and cross-user access.
Recheck retrieval and answer quality before rollout.
slides.note: The source expands its single-turn golden set when adding memory. Existing single-turn success does not demonstrate conversational quality. Use explicit reference identities rather than evaluating fluency alone. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/orchestration-and-application-logic.
slides.lesson_title: Orchestration and Application Logic

slides.title: Practical / model the memory contract offline
body: Inspect a bounded fixture and a failed-rewrite fallback.
Explain why the simulation is not a durable session service.
slides.note: This educational simulation uses no LLM or database and does not add conversation memory to the API. Learners submit an implementation plan naming storage, authorization, token budgeting and multi-turn tests. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/orchestration-and-application-logic.
slides.lesson_title: Orchestration and Application Logic

slides.title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems
slides.note: This section follows the lesson Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems. Teach the concept first, then distinguish the existing NexaAssist implementation from proposed extensions. The slides paraphrase the source rather than reproduce its text. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Use two kinds of observation
body: System health: latency, failures, tokens and priced cost.
Answer quality: grounding, relevance and correct scope.
A healthy system can still produce a harmful answer.
slides.note: APM spans diagnose infrastructure; semantic evaluation and human review diagnose meaning. Neither substitutes for the other. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Trace one answer to its artifacts
body: Prompt ID, version and content fingerprint.
Evidence references and optional Datadog span ID.
slides.note: The response carries provenance, and feedback preserves the submitted response. Client-supplied provenance is useful context but is not tamper-proof attestation. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Sampled judging is an explicit choice
body: The sample rate is configurable; zero disables sampled judging.
slides.code:
def should_sample(answer: AnswerResponse, settings: Settings) -> bool:
    """Only answered responses carry claims to check; abstentions are skipped."""
    return answer.status == "answered" and random.random() < settings.live_eval_sample_rate


async def score_sampled_answer(
    request: RetrieveRequest, answer: AnswerResponse, settings: Settings
) -> None:
    """Background reference-free judging of live traffic; failures are logged, never raised.
slides.note: Open app/services/evaluation.py and locate def should_sample. Read the displayed excerpt in context; it is taken directly from the application. The sample rate is configurable; zero disables sampled judging. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Know what sampled faithfulness measures
body: Sampling answered requests adds model cost.
The current judge uses cited quotes as its context.
This is a grounding proxy with limited observation.
slides.note: A low sample count can miss failures. A quoted passage may omit other retrieved context, so do not call the proxy an exhaustive hallucination detector. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Quality is maintained in three layers
body: Human review assesses context and newly observed failures.
Governance controls changes to meaning and risk.
slides.note: The layers complement each other. LLM-based evaluations can vary even in an offline run; do not call them deterministic simply because the dataset is fixed. Preserve judge versions and compare a sample to reviewed human assessments. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: The review queue needs the exact interaction
body: Link the input, evidence references, output and versions.
Prioritize explicit complaints and representative samples.
Review the source before accepting the correction.
slides.note: The stored response is client supplied and does not prove server execution. The authenticated export reads the accepted institution-scoped review and requires a separately curated GoldenAnswer. It returns an audit bundle without changing the shipped dataset or establishing semantic truth. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Human feedback is a signal
body: A thumbs-down may mean wrong scope or poor wording.
Review source, context and answer before accepting it.
Never turn raw feedback directly into a golden answer.
slides.note: The feedback queue has pending, accepted and rejected states. Reviewer authentication and idempotent submission support workflow, while domain verification supplies truth. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: The human review loop has owners
body: Review → proposed golden case → regression replay
slides.note: This is our workshop interpretation of the course feedback loop. Each transition needs evidence and an owner, especially where policy meaning changes. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Practical 2 / inspect feedback behavior
body: Run feedback, sampling and comparison tests.
Follow reviewer authentication and review transitions.
Explain why accepted feedback still needs a verified reference.
slides.note: The existing API stores client-submitted response data. The class should not treat a submitted provenance object as a trusted replay of server execution. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Export a reviewed regression case
body: Accepted review + curated answer → golden case.
Keep the review bundle beside the validated JSONL.
slides.note: POST /feedback/{feedback_id}/golden requires reviewer authentication, an accepted server-side review and a separate GoldenAnswer for the same input. Submitted answers/corrections are never copied automatically. The API returns the case and audit data without editing datasets. The SME verifies source accuracy; existing category mappings remain unchanged. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Governance follows the change’s meaning
body: Engineering reviews code and operational behavior.
A domain expert reviews policy meaning and golden answers.
The designated owner approves real data use and risk.
slides.note: These are proposed workshop responsibilities. Record actual names and approval dates for a real release instead of inventing an organization-specific approval matrix. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Watch both semantic and operational drift
body: Topic shifts can expose gaps in the golden set.
Policy updates can invalidate otherwise stable answers.
Judge changes can move scores without application changes.
slides.note: NexaAssist has comparison functions and sampled judging, not a complete semantic drift detector. Treat changing scores as evidence to investigate, aligning datasets and judge configuration before assigning cause. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Practical 1 / run an incident safely
body: No traffic → every required SLO is not_measured.
Scenario failures: p95 latency and hallucination proxy.
slides.note: The scenario sets p95 to 2500 ms and the proxy to 0.15 under the shipped placeholder gates. Nothing is deployed and no database is changed. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: A regression needs a comparable baseline
body: Investigate cases and configuration before interpreting it.
slides.note: These are scenario scores. Comparison now requires matching dataset fingerprints, unique case IDs, judge model/version and Ragas version, with identical finite metric sets. Regenerate legacy reports. Per-case flips can block a release even when averages hide them. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Exercise / remove an observation
body: Set sampled_count=0 and the proxy to None.
Explain what evidence is needed before clearing an incident.
slides.note: Learners should preserve the incident until relevant observations support recovery. Operational latency recovery alone does not prove restored semantic quality. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Practical 3 / rehearse rollback
body: Hold candidate → preserve evidence → restore known-good set
Replay failing and golden cases → measure representative traffic
Document owner decision and follow-up regression case
slides.note: This is a tabletop, not a deployment script. Restore compatible code, prompts, models and retrieval stores; rehearse the exact operational switch before any real release. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: A new index name is not a data snapshot
body: Ingestion mutates the configured chunk collection.
Parent sections must also match the candidate corpus.
Blue/green requires isolated compatible stores and a tested switch.
slides.note: Do not imply that changing VECTOR_INDEX_NAME alone performs safe rollback. Separate parent data matters because generation uses those sections after retrieval. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: What belongs in the release file
body: Offline quality report and representative SLO evidence.
Approver, rollback owner, known limits and incident links.
slides.note: This workspace copy has no Git metadata. Do not invent a commit or release tag; use actual identifiers from the environment where the release is built. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/quality-human-in-the-loop-and-governance-systems.
slides.lesson_title: Quality, Human-in-the-Loop, and Governance Systems

slides.title: Future Directions in LLMOps
slides.note: This section follows the lesson Future Directions in LLMOps. Teach the concept first, then distinguish the existing NexaAssist implementation from proposed extensions. The slides paraphrase the source rather than reproduce its text. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/future-directions-in-llmops.
slides.lesson_title: Future Directions in LLMOps

slides.title: Agents add actions and new failure modes
body: Tool access needs permissions and an allowlist.
Loops need iteration, time and cost bounds.
Side effects need isolation, audit and recovery.
slides.note: Agents are future scope here. The existing read-only RAG assistant does not become an agent merely because the course discusses tool loops. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/future-directions-in-llmops.
slides.lesson_title: Future Directions in LLMOps

slides.title: Bound an agent before granting actions
body: Limit steps, time, token spend and tool permissions.
Isolate side effects and preserve an audit trail.
Evaluate tool choice, arguments and recovery behavior.
slides.note: A read-only assistant becomes materially different when it can modify a record. The source names iteration caps, allowlists and sandboxed execution. These are design requirements for a future layer, not controls implemented by the current chain. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/future-directions-in-llmops.
slides.lesson_title: Future Directions in LLMOps

slides.title: Multimodal inputs expand the ingestion boundary
body: OCR or vision extraction introduces interpretation errors.
Images and audio can carry identifiers or instructions.
Queue expensive processing and evaluate the extracted evidence.
slides.note: A text-first index can simplify downstream retrieval but still needs modality-specific validation and privacy review. Adding image input is not merely changing an embedding model. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/future-directions-in-llmops.
slides.lesson_title: Future Directions in LLMOps

slides.title: Model distillation introduces a training lifecycle
body: Curate teacher traces into reviewed training data.
Evaluate a smaller student on quality and safety cases.
Version the dataset, model and rollback decision.
slides.note: The 4D phase named Distill is broader than knowledge distillation. Keep those two meanings distinct. A smaller model can reduce resource use, but improvement must be measured for the task. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/future-directions-in-llmops.
slides.lesson_title: Future Directions in LLMOps

slides.title: Edge execution shifts the operational trade-off
body: Local inference can reduce network disclosure and round trips.
Device differences affect performance and version consistency.
Telemetry, updates and recovery need a new design.
slides.note: Avoid the source’s absolute “near-zero latency” phrasing. On-device models can be slow or constrained, and local processing does not guarantee that every feature avoids external calls. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/future-directions-in-llmops.
slides.lesson_title: Future Directions in LLMOps

slides.title: The lifecycle survives a change in capabilities
body: Define the new permission and data boundaries.
Evaluate before deployment and version the artifacts.
Observe failures and close the reviewed feedback loop.
slides.note: Agents, multimodality, distillation and edge execution introduce different engineering work. The operating principles continue to apply; capability should follow a concrete use case and a measurable acceptance plan. Source lesson: https://www.educative.io/courses/llmops/future-directions-in-llmops.

slides.title: Final gate / defend the decision
body: Submit manifest, retrieval experiment and golden review.
Attach quality/SLO reports and an incident write-up.
State release, hold or unmeasured with supporting evidence.
slides.note: A successful class demonstrates engineering judgment and reproducible exercises. It does not certify a real production environment that has not been tested.

slides.title: Operate the loop, not just the endpoint
body: Version the artifacts that change answers.
Measure evidence, meaning and operations separately.
Turn reviewed failures into durable regression cases.
slides.note: Close by asking each pair what they would investigate first after an incorrect fee answer. Point learners to the source course and local handouts for continued practice.
